title: Scale & Precision: Vector Hosting tradeoffs - HorizonX discovery
topics: hosting options: hosted vs dedicated vs private VPC
summary: Discovery call with HorizonX to map current vector search stack (Elastic + FAISS experiments), quantify throughput/tail-latency targets, and evaluate Redwood hosting paths (hosted, dedicated, private). Main concerns: 99.9th percentile latency under 120ms for rerank path at peak QPS, cost of high-dim embeddings, and security/data residency for EU customers. Agreed next steps: run a small throughput benchmark, share security pack + pricing ballpark, align on POC success metrics.

transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2029-04-11
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~58m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Noah Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (HorizonX), Ethan Morales (HorizonX), Sara Lopez (HorizonX), Devon Kim (HorizonX PM)

Auto-Summary (auto-gen, may be rough): Discussed embedding dims, throughput targets, existing Elastic + FAISS setup, hybrid BM25->rerank flow, hosting options including VPC/private, agreed to run benchmarks and share security docs.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. quick intro — I'm Maya, AE for the account, Liam and Noah are our solution engineers. Priya, Ethan, do you want to intro your roles?
[00:10] Priya Nair: yeah, thanks. I'm Priya, head of search at HorizonX. we run commerce search across us/eu and we're trying to tighten results and personalization latency.
[00:20] Ethan Morales: Ethan, lead ML eng. I own embeddings and rerank models. we've been experimenting with faiss clusters and some managed vector dbs.
[00:27] Sara Lopez: Sara, infra. i'll own any network/VPC bits.
[00:30] Devon Kim: Devon - product, i'll be the stakeholder for success criteria.
[00:36] Maya Chen: great. high-level goal today — map your current pipeline, constraints, and what success looks like for a POC. then we'll suggest hosting path (hosted vs dedicated vs private). sound good?
[00:46] Priya Nair: yeah. we want to reduce manual tuning, get predictable tail latency, and keep costs reasonable. also EU data residency is a must for some customers.
[00:54] Liam O'Connor: quick clarifying q — when you say predictable tail, do you have a 99p or 99.9p target? and is that for the full search + rerank end-to-end or just the rerank model?
[01:05] Priya Nair: both ideally. but for launch i'd say rerank 99.9p under 120ms target, end-to-end for search under 250ms. if that's unrealistic at scale we'll prioritize rerank.
[01:15] Maya Chen: good, that helps. Ethan, can you walk through current flow and volumes?
[01:20] Ethan Morales: sure. current flow is query -> ES BM25 shortlist (top 200) -> embed/rerank using a 1,536-dim encoder (we're using HF model forks), then we do dot-product scoring against dense embeddings. we experimented with a faiss shard for recall but seen tail issues. avg QPS is 80 steady, spikes to 450 during promotions. doc corpus is ~25M product records but active index for rerank is ~4M.
[01:45] Noah Patel: 1,536 dims is high. curious why chosen — more semantic precision?
[01:50] Ethan Morales: yeah, we moved from 768 to 1,536 to improve nuance. precision gains are real but cost and compute are up. we also saw kv-cache sizes blow up for long sessions.
[02:05] Liam O'Connor: makes sense. on the Redwood side we typically advise testing across dims — 768/1,024/1,536 — and quantization options. quantized (8-bit/4-bit) embeddings often preserve ranking for many use cases and reduce memory and throughput cost.
[02:20] Priya Nair: can you quantize embeddings at index-time? we want to keep original vectors for some analytic work but serve quantized for production.
[02:28] Liam O'Connor: yeah you can. common pattern: keep high-precision backup storage, but the production serving layer uses quantized index for live queries. Redwood supports that pattern, and we can route queries to fallback high-precision nodes for specific cohorts.
[02:41] [crosstalk] Ethan Morales: fallback nodes meaning dedicated capacity? or hosted can do that too?
[02:47] Maya Chen: both. Hosted can be set up with variants and automated fallback rules — if tail latency spikes we'll route to a cheaper but higher-latency variant or to Dedicated pools depending on config. Dedicated gives you more predictable tail at higher price but private VPC adds network constraints.
[03:05] Devon Kim: talking about Dedicated — what's the typical lead time and what's involved on our side?
[03:10] Noah Patel: lead time is typically days to provision reserved GPU pools once contract/commit is in place. you'd need some onboarding for private networking and credentials for private. for on-prem it's longer.
[03:20] Sara Lopez: for VPC peering we need static egress IPs and IP allowlist. can Redwood do peering into our VPC or do you do NAT egress?
[03:28] Liam O'Connor: we support both. options: managed peering (VPC peering) or IP allowlist with private link - depends on cloud provider. We'll include exact networking playbook in the security pack.
[03:40] Priya Nair: any examples of customers with EU data residency + dedicated? we need SLA and audit logs for some customers.
[03:47] Maya Chen: yes, several. Redwood Private (VPC) option supports regional control plane and audit logs, KMS integration for key rotations, and we publish SOC2/ISO artifacts. we'll attach anonymized case studies.
[03:59] Ethan Morales: great. now on retrieval: we currently fetch top 200 from ES — is that a common shortlist size?
[04:06] Liam O'Connor: 100-500 is common. shortlist size drives rerank cost linearly. with a 1,536-dim model and QPS 450 you quickly saturate GPU tokens if you rerank all 200 at peak. tradeoff: smaller shortlist + better embed dim or hybrid rerank (sparse+dense scoring).
[04:25] Priya Nair: we tried 50 shortlist and saw a dip in recall for long-tail queries.
[04:30] Noah Patel: that's where rerank quality vs throughput balancing comes in. we can do a cascade: lexical-first (BM25) for high precision common queries, then dense rerank for ambiguous queries. Redwood supports routing and A/B canarying for those policies.
[04:45] [00:04:47] Ethan Morales: how does Redwood handle continuous batching for rerank? our current infra has variable burstiness so batching could help but tail latency for a single query is critical.
[04:55] Liam O'Connor: our runtime uses dynamic batching with latency SLO awareness — it will batch up to a max while keeping per-request latency targets. so under steady high throughput you get great amortization; under spiky single-request patterns it prioritizes latency. There are knobs to tune batch windows and max tokens per batch.
[05:15] Devons (sic) Devon Kim: any particular kernel optimizations for 1,536 dims? I've heard some runtimes are better at multiples of 128 etc.
[05:23] Noah Patel: yes, memory layout and kernel selection matters. our compilation layer picks optimized kernels for shape and hardware. sometimes reducing to 1,024 dims yields better real-world throughput if model accuracy doesn't drop much.
[05:35] Priya Nair: curious about cost math — can you ballpark cost difference between hosted and dedicated for our spike profile?
[05:42] Maya Chen: rough rule: hosted is lower up-front, pay-per-use — good if you can accept occasional tail variance. Dedicated is more predictable and cheaper at sustained high QPS (like your 450 spikes if sustained). we'll produce a modeling sheet with break-even points.
[05:58] Ethan Morales: for the POC — what success metrics should we use?
[06:02] Maya Chen: agreed metrics: rerank 99.9p <= 120ms, end-to-end median < 250ms, semantic relevance delta over baseline (mrr or ndcg improvement target), and cost per 1k queries under a threshold.
[06:15] Priya Nair: for relevance improvements we'll share a small labeled eval set.
[06:19] Liam O'Connor: perfect, we'll use that for offline eval and shadow rerank.
[06:24] [00:06:28] Ethan Morales: about vector DBs — we have faiss shards right now, but we're evaluating managed index solutions. how does Redwood integrate with external vector DBs versus using Redwood's embedding store?
[06:36] Noah Patel: Redwood can operate in two ways: 1) route calls to an external vector DB (we have adapters for Pinecone/Milvus/Weaviate/FAISS dockerized endpoints) so you keep your index, or 2) use Redwood's managed index layer with built-in quantization, sharding, and autoscaling. Many customers start with an adapter to validate ops before migrating to managed indexes for simplified ops.
[06:59] Priya Nair: if we keep faiss ourselves, will Redwood's runtime still handle rerank batching and model serving?
[07:06] Liam O'Connor: yes — you can keep your index; Redwood will call your nearest index endpoint for vector recall and then run model serving for rerank. the key is network locality — for low tail latency you want the rerank model colocated or in same region as the index.
[07:20] Sara Lopez: so if we peered VPCs in eu-central and us-west, that helps keep RTT low?
[07:25] Liam O'Connor: exactly. for EU residency we can run Dedicated in eu-central and keep index + rerank in region.
[07:32] Priya Nair: can we do hybrid search (BM25 + dense) in one flow with Redwood do you have an example?
[07:38] Noah Patel: yes. you can run lexical priority to get top K, then perform a dense recall against the managed index and merge scores with learned weights, or do a two-stage rerank where dense score is used only for top candidates. Redwood Console supports route definitions and debug traces for that flow.
[07:55] Ethan Morales: interesting. what about cold-start indexing and real-time updates? our product catalog changes fast during promotions.
[08:02] Liam O'Connor: Redwood's index supports partial updates and near-real-time ingest. there's a configurable freshness window and immediate small-batch inserts for high-priority items. we'll share docs on expected indexing latency by config.
[08:14] Devon Kim: we have compliance questions: how are embeddings treated for data exfil protection? we don't want proprietary product signals sent to third-party models.
[08:22] Maya Chen: good question. Redwood supports customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM), private deployments where models run in your VPC, and can disable external telemetry. Also audit logs and tenant isolation are available for Dedicated and Private. We'll include the controls matrix in the security pack.
[08:38] Priya Nair: can we run our own quantized rerank model in Redwood Private if we want to keep weights on-prem?
[08:44] Noah Patel: yes, Private supports bringing your own model binaries (with license constraints) and on-prem GPU attach. there are extra ops steps but it's supported.
[08:53] [00:08:55] Ethan Morales: for benchmarking — what does Redwood need from us to reproduce realistic traffic?
[09:00] Liam O'Connor: sample queries distribution, QPS profiles (steady vs burst), sample of candidate lists size distribution, and embedding dim. we'll provide a replay/benchmark harness that can call your BM25 + rerank path or proxy it if you prefer.
[09:13] Maya Chen: we'll send that harness after the call. expected run: small smoke with 100k docs then a scaled run with 4M active docs.
[09:21] Priya Nair: any pitfalls when measuring 99.9p — should we measure client-side or server-side?
[09:26] Noah Patel: measure both. server-side gives you runtime service latency; client-side includes network and any proxying. for SLOs we recommend client-side (user-experienced) but include server-side as part of root cause.
[09:37] Ethan Morales: what's Redwood's behavior under memory pressure for big kv cache? do you evict aggressively?
[09:42] Liam O'Connor: runtime manages KV cache with LRU-ish policies and allows you to pin critical keys. eviction policies and cache sizes are configurable per-deployment.
[09:53] Priya Nair: I want to talk about cost for long-tail personalization — if we maintain user vectors and rerank per user session, that could explode cost. any patterns?
[10:02] Noah Patel: common patterns: cohort-based rerank (only rerank for segments with high conversion), online caching of recent user vectors, and async background pre-scoring for users with high activity. Redwood Optimize can suggest batching/cache windows to reduce unit cost.
[10:19] Devon Kim: ok, let's talk timeline — assuming we like the results, how long to a pilot?
[10:24] Maya Chen: pilot can start within 2 weeks post-benchmark: initial scope 4 weeks where we run isolated traffic, collect metrics, then expand. Dedicated procurement adds contracting time.
[10:33] [00:10:35] Priya Nair: are there examples of companies switching from faiss self-hosted to Redwood managed index for cost savings?
[10:41] Maya Chen: yes, a few retail customers saw 20-40% lower op cost after moving to managed indexes + quantization due to autoscaling and consolidation of index resources. we'll include a case summary.
[10:53] Ethan Morales: any limits on embedding dimensions in Redwood managed index? we use 1,536 now.
[10:59] Liam O'Connor: no hard limits, but memory/perf considerations apply. we recommend a dimension sweep as part of POC. There are also techniques like product quantization that make large dims feasible.
[11:12] Sara Lopez: for VPC/private deployments, what level of telemetry can you keep out? we need zero external calls for a subset of customers.
[11:19] Noah Patel: in Private you can disable telemetry and external dns resolution; audit logs are local and you control key material. we'll detail the controls.
[11:27] [00:11:30] Devon Kim: ok time to recap and next steps?
[11:31] Maya Chen: recap: Redwood will send security docs, benchmark harness, pricing snapshot. HorizonX will share sample queries and index stats and run the smoke benchmark. follow-up technical POC scoping next week.
[11:44] Priya Nair: thanks — appreciate the clarity.
[11:47] Ethan Morales: quick q — do you have pre-built dashboards for rerank/recall metrics?
[11:51] Noah Patel: yes, Redwood Console has per-route dashboards, token-level cost, latency percentiles, and an eval harness to compare ndcg/mrr. we'll share screenshots.
[12:02] Maya Chen: i'll get the pack sent today. thanks everyone.
[12:06] Priya Nair: thanks — bye.

END OF TRANSCRIPT
